svg.text: Atherosclerosis and thrombus
yellow: deposits of fat, cholesterol, fibrin,
smooth muscle cells and debris narrow the artery
brown: a thrombus (clot) may block it; a thrombus
carried elsewhere is an embolus (thromboembolism)
arteriosclerosis: calcium hardens the wall, so the
artery cannot expand and the heart works harder
Angiography
a catheter is guided through the large arteries
to the coronary openings; a contrast dye visible
on X-ray is injected, and the angiogram shows
where a clot narrows the lumen
a guiding catheter can then carry guide wires
and balloon catheters into the artery
Coronary bypass
a healthy vessel from the leg, arm, chest
or abdomen is joined above and below
the blockage so blood bypasses it
does not cure the atherosclerosis itself:
stopping smoking, less fat, more activity,
control of blood pressure and diabetes
Angioplasty and stenting
1. a wire catheter is passed through
the narrowed section under X-ray; a
small balloon on it is inflated to dilate
the artery; dye confirms the result
2. a stent, an expandable stainless
steel mesh tube on the balloon, is
expanded with it and left in place
to hold the artery open
From narrowed artery to failing heart
angina pectoris: chest pain on stress or exertion when oxygen
demand exceeds delivery; a warning of a future attack
myocardial infarction (heart attack): heart muscle dies when a
coronary artery is blocked; recovery is possible if the area is small
congestive heart failure: a weakened heart cannot keep up the
flow, and blood is retained in the heart and lungs (no chest pain)
Red: artery wall. Pale: lumen. Green: the bypass graft. Grey: balloon and stent. Schematic, not to scale.
Open or beating-heart surgery is done while the heart is still beating. A stroke is the same blockage in a vessel of the brain.
